# Appendix B — Event Ledger {.unnumbered}

A dated chronology of the events this book turns on, from the Spanish occupation
of Alta California to the present.

## Method

An event earns a place here if it meets one of four tests.

1. It moved a chokepoint — created one, captured one, or destroyed one.
2. It converted public money or public authority into private control.
3. It changed who could enter the elite, or how.
4. It is a date a reader would want to check.

Events that are famous but structurally inert are omitted. Events that are
obscure but load-bearing are included.

## What changed in this edition

The ledger inherited from the drafts carried 47 events tagged `[S1]`–`[S87]`. The
key those tags referred to was not preserved with the drafts and could not be
reconstructed, so the tags have been removed rather than left as decoration. Each
row now carries a verification status instead, and the underlying claims are
tracked in `_project/research-log.md`.

Three other changes. Two rows were removed because they were not events — they
recorded a company's anniversary and a firm restating its own founding date,
which are artefacts of the drafting process rather than history. The ledger has
been extended backwards to 1769, since the original began at the Gold Rush and
this book's argument begins eighty years earlier. And the secession-and-route
sequence of 1853 to 1862 has been added, since it is the causal hinge of the book
and no draft contained it.

**Status values.** `VERIFIED` means the claim is supported by a source recorded in
the research log. `NEEDS SOURCE` means the event is drafted and the citation is
outstanding. `CONTESTED` means historians genuinely disagree, and the text handles
it under the rule in `_project/voice.md`.

## Spanish and Mexican California (1769–1847)

| Date | Event | Why it matters | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1769-07-16 | Mission San Diego de Alcalá founded; Spanish occupation of Alta California begins | Begins the mission-presidio-pueblo system: California's first apparatus of labour and record. | VERIFIED |
| 1776-06-29 | Mission San Francisco de Asís founded at what is now 320 Dolores Street | Anchors the Spanish claim to the Pacific's greatest natural harbour. Oldest intact building in the city. | VERIFIED |
| 1821-09-27 | Mexican independence; Alta California transfers to Mexico | Territory transferred without administrative capacity; land grants replace governance. | VERIFIED |
| 1834-08-09 | Secularisation of the missions begins | Largest land transfer in California history. Restitution promised to neophytes; almost none delivered. | VERIFIED |

## Conquest, Gold, and Statehood (1848–1852)

| Date | Event | Why it matters | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1848-01-24 | Gold discovered at Sutter's Mill | Detonates the incentive structure of the Pacific coast. Marshall and Sutter both ruined by it. | VERIFIED |
| 1848-02-02 | Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo cedes California to the United States | Converts occupation into legal ownership. Signed nine days after the gold discovery, in ignorance of it. | VERIFIED |
| 1849-10-13 | California constitution signed at Colton Hall | Statehood organised without congressional authorisation; slavery prohibited. | VERIFIED |
| 1850-03-30 | Foreign Miners' Tax enacted | Extraction from Mexican, Chilean and Peruvian miners. First appearance of a recurring Californian manoeuvre. | VERIFIED |
| 1850-04-22 | Act for the Government and Protection of Indians | Permits arrest of Indians deemed loitering and indenture of Indigenous children. Forced labour in a free state. | VERIFIED |
| 1850-09-09 | California admitted as a state under the Compromise of 1850 | Places California on the sectional chessboard from its first day, which decides the railroad route in 1862. | VERIFIED |
| 1851-03-03 | California Land Act establishes the land commission | Places burden of proof on Mexican grant-holders. Transfers land by procedure rather than by seizure. | VERIFIED |

## The Route and the Railroad (1853–1883)

| Date | Event | Why it matters | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1853-03-03 | Congress appropriates $150,000 for Pacific railroad surveys | Four corridors surveyed. Every field commander reports his own route is best; Congress cannot decide. | VERIFIED |
| 1853-12-30 | Gadsden Purchase signed | Acquires the strip required for a 32nd-parallel southern railroad route. | VERIFIED |
| 1861-01-21 | Jefferson Davis speaks for a transcontinental railroad days before leaving the Senate | 'To couple with bonds of iron the people of the Pacific with the valley of the Mississippi.' His departure is what makes it possible. | VERIFIED |
| 1861-06-28 | Central Pacific Railroad incorporated | Four merchants and an engineer. Judah is bought out and dies in 1863. | NEEDS SOURCE |
| 1862-07-01 | Pacific Railway Act signed | Passes only after secession empties the Southern seats. Land grants and 30-year bonds at 6 per cent. Union Pacific is the first federally chartered corporation since the Second Bank. | VERIFIED |
| 1867-06-25 | Chinese workers strike on the Sierra grade | Several thousand men demand pay parity and shorter tunnel hours. Broken within a week by cutting off food. | VERIFIED |
| 1869-05-10 | Golden spike completes the transcontinental railroad | A public work becomes a private monopoly. The Chinese workforce is absent from the photograph. | VERIFIED |
| 1876-01-01 | Southern Pacific completes the line to Los Angeles | Consolidation of rail power; the company begins deciding which towns exist. | NEEDS SOURCE |
| 1880-05-11 | Mussel Slough shootout | Seven dead in a dispute over railroad land titles. The physical edge of legal architecture. | VERIFIED |
| 1882-05-06 | Chinese Exclusion Act signed | First federal law barring a nationality. The men who built the Sierra grade are prohibited from the country they connected. | VERIFIED |

## The Institution (1884–1918)

| Date | Event | Why it matters | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1884-03-13 | Leland Stanford Jr. dies in Florence | The university follows. Corrects the 1885 date given in some drafts. | VERIFIED |
| 1885-11-11 | Stanford Founding Grant executed | Self-perpetuating board, insulated from politics, endowed with land that cannot be sold. The clause that produces the research park in 1951. | VERIFIED |
| 1886-05-10 | Santa Clara County v. Southern Pacific decided | Decided on narrow grounds; the reporter's headnote records corporate personhood. Doctrine develops over subsequent decades. | VERIFIED |
| 1886-05-10 | Yick Wo v. Hopkins decided | A law fair on its face but administered with an unequal hand violates equal protection. Brought by Chinese laundry operators. | VERIFIED |
| 1891-10-01 | Stanford University opens | Free tuition, coeducational, practical curriculum. First president is a leading eugenicist. | VERIFIED |
| 1893-06-21 | Leland Stanford dies during the Panic of 1893 | Estate frozen; the federal government sues for $15 million. The university nearly closes. | VERIFIED |
| 1898-03-28 | United States v. Wong Kim Ark decided | Establishes birthright citizenship, on a case brought by a man born in San Francisco to Chinese parents. | VERIFIED |
| 1900-11-12 | Edward Ross forced out of Stanford | Founding controversy of American academic freedom, at a university built by a railroad, over criticism of railroads. | VERIFIED |
| 1905-02-28 | Jane Stanford dies in Honolulu | Cause contested. The institution continues without structural change, which is the load-bearing fact. | CONTESTED |
| 1906-04-18 | San Francisco earthquake and fire | Stanford badly damaged and absorbs it. Assets were land and endowment, not buildings. | VERIFIED |
| 1909-04-26 | California sterilisation law enacted | California performs roughly a third of the recorded US total. Law stands until 1979. | VERIFIED |
| 1913-05-19 | California Alien Land Law | Bars aliens ineligible for citizenship from owning agricultural land; aimed at Japanese farmers. | VERIFIED |

## The Archive State and the War (1919–1950)

| Date | Event | Why it matters | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1919-06-01 | Hoover funds what becomes the Hoover War Collection | $50,000 and agents in a collapsed Europe. California acquires memory infrastructure. | VERIFIED |
| 1925-01-01 | Stanford Graduate School of Business founded | The management credential formalised. Steinbeck leaves without a degree the same year. | VERIFIED |
| 1936-10-05 | Steinbeck's 'The Harvest Gypsies' begins publication | An administrative record of a labour system compiled by someone with no institutional interest in the outcome. | VERIFIED |
| 1939-01-01 | Hewlett-Packard founded at 367 Addison Avenue | The garage is real and it is not the explanation. Terman told them to stay. | VERIFIED |
| 1942-02-19 | Executive Order 9066 | Incarceration of some 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry. Property lost at distress prices; the transfer had beneficiaries. | VERIFIED |
| 1945-07-01 | Vannevar Bush delivers 'Science, the Endless Frontier' | The intellectual case for permanent federal funding of basic research through universities. | VERIFIED |
| 1946-08-01 | Office of Naval Research established | Fills the five-year gap before the NSF. American basic science funding is architected with a service branch as founding patron. | VERIFIED |
| 1946-11-06 | Stanford Research Institute established | Owned by the university. The ownership is what the 1969 protests turn on. | NEEDS SOURCE |

## The Valley (1951–1979)

| Date | Event | Why it matters | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1951-01-01 | Stanford Industrial Park opens | First university-owned industrial park in the US. Direct consequence of the 1885 prohibition on selling land. | NEEDS SOURCE |
| 1956-01-01 | Lockheed Missiles and Space opens in Sunnyvale | Becomes the county's largest employer and is absent from the region's origin story. | NEEDS SOURCE |
| 1956-02-01 | Shockley Semiconductor opens in Mountain View | Located there because his mother lived there. | VERIFIED |
| 1957-09-18 | The eight resign from Shockley; Fairchild Semiconductor follows | The spinoff becomes the Valley's reproductive mechanism, enabled by California's refusal to enforce non-competes. | VERIFIED |
| 1959-01-01 | Planar process developed at Fairchild | Makes the integrated circuit manufacturable. The advantage lives in people and therefore walks. | VERIFIED |
| 1962-11-01 | Knight secures Tiger distribution rights in Kobe | Blue Ribbon Sports invented on the spot. The company began as a Stanford class paper. | VERIFIED |
| 1963-01-01 | Fairchild opens assembly operations in Hong Kong | The offshore turn in semiconductors, in the same years Knight is arranging it in footwear. | NEEDS SOURCE |
| 1965-04-19 | Moore's law published | A coordination device rather than a prediction. Sets the industry's clock for half a century. | VERIFIED |
| 1968-12-09 | Engelbart's demonstration at the Fall Joint Computer Conference | Mouse, hypertext, windows, collaborative editing. Federally funded and commercially uncaptured. | VERIFIED |
| 1969-04-09 | Students occupy the Applied Electronics Laboratory | Nine days. They print the classified research they find. The senate bans classified work on 24 April. | VERIFIED |
| 1969-05-16 | Police tear-gas students protesting the SRI divestment | They had asked the university to take responsibility. It took its name off the door instead. | VERIFIED |
| 1969-10-29 | First ARPANET message, UCLA to SRI | The system crashes after two letters. The internet's first word is 'lo'. | VERIFIED |
| 1970-01-01 | Trustees set terms for the SRI divestment | SRI sold to itself for 1 per cent of gross revenues up to $25 million. Pressure produced reorganisation, not reform. | VERIFIED |
| 1972-01-01 | Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia Capital founded on Sand Hill Road | Both founded by operators from the semiconductor industry, four minutes from the campus supplying the deal flow. | VERIFIED |
| 1975-03-05 | First Homebrew Computer Club meeting | Circulating culture, enclosed within about five years. | VERIFIED |
| 1979-02-01 | ERISA prudent man rule clarified | Admits pension money to venture funds. The public-money leg of the capital chokepoint. | VERIFIED |

## Platforms (1980–2005)

| Date | Event | Why it matters | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1980-08-12 | IBM Personal Computer development; MS-DOS licensed non-exclusively | The most valuable clause never inserted. Hardware commoditises; the operating system does not. | NEEDS SOURCE |
| 1980-10-14 | Genentech IPO | Biology financed like software, on a Stanford and UCSF patent. | VERIFIED |
| 1980-12-12 | Bayh-Dole Act enacted | Universities take title to federally funded inventions. Answers the question Act II left open. | VERIFIED |
| 1995-04-30 | NSFNET backbone decommissioned; the network passes to commercial operators | Thirty years of public investment transferred without compensation, equity, or public debate. | VERIFIED |
| 1995-08-09 | Netscape IPO | Built on Mosaic, developed at a public university on federal funding. | VERIFIED |
| 1996-02-08 | Section 230 enacted | Twenty-six words. The legal foundation of the platform economy. | VERIFIED |
| 1998-09-04 | Google incorporated | Their published paper argues ad-funded search will be biased against users. Stanford owns the PageRank patent. | VERIFIED |
| 2002-10-03 | eBay acquires PayPal | About $1.5 billion. The product was payments; the durable asset was the address book. | VERIFIED |

## The Open Era (2006–2025)

| Date | Event | Why it matters | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2006-03-14 | Amazon Web Services launches | Computing as a metered utility. Within fifteen years much of the internet runs on three providers. | VERIFIED |
| 2006-11-16 | Nvidia introduces CUDA | A software ecosystem accumulated fifteen years before there was a market for it. The switching cost that holds the position. | VERIFIED |
| 2012-04-09 | Facebook acquires Instagram | About $1 billion for a company with no revenue. Buying the competitor before it is one. | VERIFIED |
| 2018-03-17 | Cambridge Analytica reporting published | The neutrality posture collapses in public. | VERIFIED |
| 2018-08-27 | UN fact-finding mission reports on Myanmar | Addresses the platform's role in the spread of hate speech. The company's own commissioned assessment follows. | VERIFIED |
| 2019-07-24 | FTC announces $5 billion Facebook privacy settlement | Largest privacy penalty the agency had imposed. | VERIFIED |
| 2020-11-03 | Proposition 22 passes in California | Over $200 million spent to exempt platforms from a classification law passed the previous year. | VERIFIED |
| 2022-08-09 | CHIPS and Science Act signed | Public money returns to semiconductors. Act II's triangle under the name of industrial policy. | VERIFIED |
| 2022-11-30 | OpenAI releases ChatGPT | Adoption figures widely cited from an investment bank estimate rather than a company disclosure. | VERIFIED |
| 2023-06-29 | Students for Fair Admissions decided | Race-conscious admissions held unlawful. What is the credential screening for? | VERIFIED |
| 2023-07-19 | Marc Tessier-Lavigne resigns as Stanford president | Review found manipulation by others in his laboratories and criticised his failure to correct the record. | VERIFIED |
| 2023-11-17 | OpenAI board removes its chief executive; reversed within five days | A governance mechanism designed to constrain commercial logic was tested once and failed. | VERIFIED |
| 2025-01-20 | Technology founders seated at the presidential inauguration | Visibility changes; substance does not. Thiel's roughly $15m to the 2022 Vance campaign is documented in FEC filings. | VERIFIED |

## Outstanding

Seven rows are marked `NEEDS SOURCE` and are the priority verification queue:
the Central Pacific's incorporation date against the articles, the Southern
Pacific's completion to Los Angeles, SRI's founding instrument, the Stanford
Industrial Park's authorisation and opening dates (sources give 1951 and 1953 and
the discrepancy is unresolved), Lockheed's Sunnyvale employment figures,
Fairchild's Hong Kong opening, and the IBM–Microsoft contract date and terms.
